# Unemployment Rate among Highly-Educated Immigrant Women by the Country of Destination

```{r}
library(ggrepel)
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(here)
library(tinytex)
```

## PART I: Clean data

### Data Source

The data used in this study come from the OECD Data Explorer\[\@oecddata\]: [https://data-explorer.oecd.org/vis?lc=en&df%5Bds%5D=dsDisseminateFinalDMZ&df%5Bid%5D=DSD_EAG_LSO_EA%40DF_LSO_NEAC_UNEMP_MIGR&df%5Bag%5D=OECD.EDU.IMEP&dq=AUS%2BAUT%2BBEL%2BCAN%2BCHL%2BCOL%2BCRI%2BCZE%2BEST%2BFRA%2BDEU%2BGRC%2BHUN%2BIRL%2BITA%2BLVA%2BLTU%2BLUX%2BMEX%2BNLD%2BNZL%2BNOR%2BPOL%2BPRT%2BSVK%2BSVN%2BESP%2BSWE%2BCHE%2BGBR%2BUSA%2BBGR%2BROU.M%2BF.Y25T34%2BY35T44%2BY55T64%2BY45T54%2BY25T64.ISCED11A_0T2%2BISCED11A_3_4%2BISCED11A_5T8....NB%2BFB......OBS...A3&lom=LASTNOBSERVATIONS&lo=1&pd=2023,2023&to%5BTIME_PERIOD%5D=true&lb=nm&vw=ov](#0){.uri}

```{r}
raw_data <- read_csv(here("data", "raw_data_1027.csv"))
```

```{r}
names(raw_data)
```

### Step 1: Cleaning the sex variable

The original SEX variable uses the codes F and M, which are recoded into female and male for readability.

```{r}
raw_data |> count(SEX)

clean_data <- 
  raw_data |>
  mutate(sex = case_when(
    SEX == "F" ~ "female",
    SEX == "M" ~ "male"
  )) |>
  select(-SEX, -any_of("Sex")) #刪掉原本的代碼欄和標籤欄以避免重複

count(clean_data, sex)
```

### Step 2: Cleaning the age variable

The original AGE variable uses codes such as Y25T34, which are recoded into readable age groups: 25–34. The code Y25T64 represents the total for all four age groups and is recoded as 25–64. The age groups are ordered from youngest to oldest.

```{r}
raw_data |> count(AGE)

clean_data <- 
  clean_data  |>
  mutate(age = case_when(
    AGE == "Y25T34" ~ "25-34",
    AGE == "Y35T44" ~ "35-44",
    AGE == "Y45T54" ~ "45-54",
    AGE == "Y55T64" ~ "55-64",
    AGE == "Y25T64" ~ "25-64"
  )) |>
  mutate(age = factor(age, levels = c("25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "25-64")))

count(clean_data, age)
```

### Step 3: Cleaning the educational attainment variable

The original ATTAINMENT_LEV variable uses ISCED 2011 codes, which are recoded into three categories: below upper secondary (ISCED11A_0T2), upper secondary (ISCED11A_3_4) and tertiary (ISCED11A_5T8)

```{r}
raw_data |> count(ATTAINMENT_LEV)

# 教育程度
clean_data <- 
  clean_data |>
  mutate(edu = case_when(
    ATTAINMENT_LEV == "ISCED11A_0T2" ~ "below upper secondary",
    ATTAINMENT_LEV == "ISCED11A_3_4" ~ "upper secondary",
    ATTAINMENT_LEV == "ISCED11A_5T8" ~ "tertiary"
  )) |>
  mutate(edu = factor(edu, levels = c("below upper secondary", "upper secondary", "tertiary")))

count(clean_data, edu)
```

### Step 4: Cleaning the country variable

The original REF_AREA variable uses three-letter country codes, which are converted into full country names (for example, CAN becomes Canada).

```{r}
raw_data |> count(REF_AREA)

# 國家對照表
country_names <- c(
  AUS = "Australia", AUT = "Austria", BEL = "Belgium", BGR = "Bulgaria",
  CAN = "Canada", CHE = "Switzerland", CHL = "Chile", COL = "Colombia",
  CRI = "Costa Rica", CZE = "Czechia", DEU = "Germany", ESP = "Spain",
  EST = "Estonia", FRA = "France", GBR = "United Kingdom", GRC = "Greece",
  HUN = "Hungary", IRL = "Ireland", ISR = "Israel", ITA = "Italy",
  LTU = "Lithuania", LUX = "Luxembourg", LVA = "Latvia", MEX = "Mexico",
  NLD = "Netherlands", NOR = "Norway", NZL = "New Zealand", 
  POL = "Poland", PRT = "Portugal", ROU = "Romania", SVK = "Slovak Republic",
  SVN = "Slovenia", SWE = "Sweden", USA = "United States"
)

# 國家
clean_data <- 
  clean_data |>
  mutate(country = unname(country_names[REF_AREA]))

count(clean_data, country)
```

### Step 5: Cleaning the birthplace variable

The original BIRTH_PLACE variable uses the codes NB and FB, which are recoded into native-born and foreign-born.

```{r}
raw_data |> count(BIRTH_PLACE)

clean_data <- 
  clean_data  |>
  mutate(birth = case_when(
    BIRTH_PLACE == "NB" ~ "native-born",
    BIRTH_PLACE == "FB" ~ "foreign-born"
  ))

count(clean_data, birth)
```

### Step 6: Cleaning the unemployment rate variable (the outcome variable of this study)

The original OBS_VALUE variable is renamed unemp_rate. It is already stored as a numeric value and is measured as a percentage of the labor force in each subgroup, so no further conversion is needed.

```{r}
count(raw_data, MEASURE, UNIT_MEASURE)
clean_data <-
  clean_data |>
  rename(unemp_rate = OBS_VALUE)
```

### Step 7: Keeping only the cleaned variables

```{r}
# 只保留整理好的變項
clean_data <-
  clean_data |>
  filter(MIGRATION_AGE %in% c("_Z", "_T")) |>
  select(country, sex, age, edu, birth, unemp_rate)
```

### Step 8: Coding countries by region

Each country is assigned to one of seven regions: North America, Latin America, Oceania, Western Europe, Northern Europe, Southern Europe and Eastern Europe.

```{r}
# 地區對照表
region_names <- c(
  "Canada" = "North America", "United States" = "North America",
  "Chile" = "Latin America", "Colombia" = "Latin America",
  "Costa Rica" = "Latin America", "Mexico" = "Latin America",
  "Australia" = "Oceania", "New Zealand" = "Oceania",
  "Austria" = "Eastern Europe", "Belgium" = "Western Europe",
  "France" = "Western Europe", "Germany" = "Western Europe",
  "Ireland" = "Western Europe", "Luxembourg" = "Western Europe",
  "Netherlands" = "Western Europe", "Switzerland" = "Western Europe",
  "United Kingdom" = "Western Europe",
  "Norway" = "Northern Europe", "Sweden" = "Northern Europe",
  "Greece" = "Southern Europe", "Italy" = "Southern Europe",
  "Portugal" = "Southern Europe", "Spain" = "Southern Europe",
  "Bulgaria" = "Eastern Europe", "Czechia" = "Eastern Europe",
  "Estonia" = "Eastern Europe", "Hungary" = "Eastern Europe",
  "Latvia" = "Eastern Europe", "Lithuania" = "Eastern Europe",
  "Poland" = "Eastern Europe", "Romania" = "Eastern Europe",
  "Slovak Republic" = "Eastern Europe", "Slovenia" = "Eastern Europe"
)

# 地區
clean_data <-
  clean_data |>
  mutate(region = unname(region_names[country]),
         region = factor(region, levels = c("North America", "Latin America", "Oceania",
                                            "Western Europe", "Northern Europe",
                                            "Southern Europe", "Eastern Europe")))
```

```{r}
head(clean_data)
```

## PART II: Tests

### Test1: This test checks that the recoded categorical variables (country, sex, age, education and birthplace) contain no missing values.

```{r}
sum(is.na(clean_data$sex)) == 0
sum(is.na(clean_data$age)) == 0
sum(is.na(clean_data$edu)) == 0
sum(is.na(clean_data$birth)) == 0
sum(is.na(clean_data$country)) == 0
```

### Test2: Since each combination of country, sex, age, education and birthplace should appear in only one row, this test checks that no combination is duplicated.

```{r}
clean_data |>
  count(country, sex, age, edu, birth) |>
  filter(n > 1)
```

```{r}
write_csv(clean_data, here("data", "cleaned_data.csv"))
```

### Missing Values

#### Patterns of missing values

The following codes are used to identify where the missing values are in the data. First, I identify which countries have missing values in the data. Next, I examine which countries have missing values for tertiary-educated women. Finally, I create a table showing, for each country, the age groups and birthplace categories in which data for tertiary-educated women are missing.

As shown in the Table1, 1) Luxembourg, Norway, and Romania have no data for either native-born or foreign-born highly-educated women. 2) Bulgaria, Hungary, Mexico, the Slovak Republic, and Slovenia have complete data for native-born women but no data for foreign-born women. 3) Costa Rica and Poland likewise have no data for foreign-born women, and their native-born data are also missing for the 45–54 and 55–64 age groups. 4) The remaining countries in the table have only scattered missing values, mostly for foreign-born women in the older age groups.

Notably, the pattern of missing values is different for the combined 25–64 age group. Countries with only one or a few missing age groups, such as the United Kingdom, Germany and New Zealand, all have data for the 25–64 group. Countries with no age-specific data for foreign-born women, such as Bulgaria and Hungary, also lack data for the combined group. There are, however, two exceptions. Although Norway has no data for any of the four age groups, it does report data for the 25–64 group for both native-born and foreign-born women. Similarly, Romania has no age-specific data for native-born women, but it does report data for native-born women aged 25–64.

#### Explaining the patterns of missing values

To explain the distribution of missing values, I reviewed the OECD’s methodological notes \[\@oecd2023methods\]. The OECD applies two criteria when deciding whether to publish a value: a reliability threshold and a confidentiality threshold. Under the reliability threshold, if the denominator of an indicator contains fewer than 30 respondents, the value is either not published or flagged as having reduced reliability. Under the confidentiality threshold, if the numerator contains fewer than three respondents, the value may be withheld for confidentiality reasons.

Based on these rules, it is possible that countries such as Bulgaria, Hungary, Poland, Romania, the Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Mexico and Costa Rica did not publish unemployment rates for foreign-born women because the number of foreign-born women in their samples was too small to meet the threshold. Similarly, because Luxembourg has a small population, its overall survey sample is likely to be small, so groups of both native-born and foreign-born women may fall below the threshold.

#### **How to adress missing values**

Because any imputed values would not reflect data actually published by the OECD, and because the situation differs from country to country, this study does not impute missing values. Luxembourg, Norway and Romania have no age-specific data for tertiary-educated women and are therefore excluded from the analyses by age group. In the analyses of the combined 25–64 age group, Norway is included because data are available for both native-born and foreign-born women, while Luxembourg is excluded. For all other countries with missing values, only combinations with values for both native-born and foreign-born women are kept when comparing the two groups. As a result, countries with no data for foreign-born women do not appear in the comparative graphs.

This approach inevitably introduces some limitations. The countries included in the final analysis are more likely to be those with larger foreign-born populations. Therefore, the descriptive results of this study may not generalise well to countries with smaller immigrant populations. In addition, fewer countries can be compared in the older age groups.

```{r}
# 哪些國家有缺失值
clean_data |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            n_missing = sum(is.na(unemp_rate))) |>
  filter(n_missing > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(n_missing))
```

```{r}
clean_data |>
  filter(sex == "female" & edu == "tertiary") |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            n_missing = sum(is.na(unemp_rate))) |>
  filter(n_missing > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(n_missing))
```

```{r}
#了解高等教育女性的缺失值發生在哪裡
#把缺失最多的國家放前面
#盧森堡、挪威、羅馬尼亞三國在本地和外國都沒有資料；保加利亞、匈牙利、墨西哥、斯洛伐克Slovak Republic、斯洛維尼亞Slovenia、哥斯大黎加、波蘭有本地資料但沒有外國資料。

missing_table <-
  clean_data |>
  filter(sex == "female", edu == "tertiary", age != "25-64", is.na(unemp_rate)) |>
  arrange(country, birth, age) |>
  group_by(country, birth) |>
  summarise(n_missing = n(),
            missing_ages = paste(age, collapse = ", "),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(country) |>
  mutate(missing_total = sum(n_missing)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(desc(missing_total), country, birth)

names(missing_table)
missing_table_short <-
  missing_table |>
  select(country, birth, n_missing, missing_ages)

kable(
  missing_table_short,
  caption = "Table 1: Missing values for tertiary-educated women",
  col.names = c("Country", "Birthplace", "Missing", "Missing age groups")
) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9, latex_options = "scale_down", full_width = FALSE) |>
  column_spec(1:4, extra_css = "white-space: nowrap;")
```

```{r}
clean_data |>
  filter(sex == "female", edu == "tertiary", age == "25-64", is.na(unemp_rate)) |>
  select(country, birth) |>
  arrange(country, birth)
```

### Graph1: Unemployment rates of native-born and foreign-born tertiary-educated women by age

Graph 1 shows the unemployment rates of native-born and foreign-born tertiary-educated women by age group. To further explore the different patterns among countries, I divided the countries into two regional groups: **North America, Oceania, Western and Northern Europe (shown in blue), and Latin America, Southern and Eastern Europe (shown in red)**. This division is based on geographic region and is intended to compare **major immigration destinations** with other regions.

Countries commonly regarded as having large immigrant populations, such as Australia, the United States, Canada and New Zealand, lie closer to the dashed line. In the 35–44 and 55–64 age groups, foreign-born women in Australia have slightly lower unemployment rates than native-born women. By contrast, in Southern and Eastern European countries such as Estonia, Portugal, Spain and Greece, foreign-born women have substantially higher unemployment rates than native-born women.

Interestingly, the data for Colombia show that among women aged 25–34, foreign-born women have a slightly lower unemployment rate than native-born women. In the 35–44 and 55–64 age groups, the unemployment rates of foreign-born and native-born women are relatively similar. However, in the 45–54 age group, foreign-born women have a much higher unemployment rate than Colombian native-born women.

```{r}
#準備沒有資料的國家
no_missing_base <-
  clean_data |>
  filter(!country %in% c("Luxembourg", "Norway", "Romania"))

plot_NF_data <-
  no_missing_base |>
  filter(sex == "female", edu == "tertiary", age != "25-64") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = birth, values_from = unemp_rate) |>
  #只留下兩欄都有數值的列。只要其中一邊是 NA，整列就被刪掉。
  filter(!is.na(`native-born`), !is.na(`foreign-born`)) |> 
  mutate(region_group = if_else(
    region %in% c("North America", "Oceania", "Western Europe", "Northern Europe"),
    "North America, Oceania, Western & Northern Europe",
    "Latin America, Southern & Eastern Europe"
  ))

ggplot(plot_NF_data, aes(x = `native-born`, y = `foreign-born`, colour = region_group)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey") +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ age) +
  labs(
    title = "Graph1: Unemployment rates of native-born and foreign-born\ntertiary-educated women by age",
    x = "Native-born (%)",
    y = "Foreign-born (%)",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "The diagonal line indicates equal unemployment rates for foreign-born and native-born women."
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = country), size = 2.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "North America, Oceania, Western & Northern Europe" = "blue",
    "Latin America, Southern & Eastern Europe" = "red"
  )) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

### Graph2: Unemployment rates of native-born and foreign-born tertiary-educated women aged 25-64

Looking at tertiary-educated women aged 25–64 as a whole, there is no country in which foreign-born women have a lower unemployment rate than native-born women. **Every country lies above the diagonal line.** These results suggest that foreign-born women may face a weaker position in the labor market than native-born women, and that tertiary education may not fully eliminate this disadvantage.

Among more developed countries, Australia, New Zealand and the United States (shown in blue) show the smallest differences between the unemployment rates of foreign-born and native-born women. However, Canada, Sweden, and France lie much further from the diagonal line, indicating a larger gap between foreign-born and native-born women. **In Canada, for example, the unemployment rate of foreign-born women is roughly double that of native-born women. This may suggest that even in countries with large immigrant populations, foreign-born women may still face greater challenges in the labor market.** Explaining this pattern would require more country-specific information, such as data on immigration policies or immigrants’ countries of origin.

Southern European, Eastern European and Latin American countries generally have higher unemployment rates, reflecting overall weaker labor market conditions. Spain shows the largest gap, with the unemployment rate of foreign-born women about 7 percentage points higher than that of native-born women. By contrast, Colombia has the highest native-born unemployment rate in the sample, but the gap between the two groups is relatively small, at around 2 percentage points. The only exception among the red countries is Czechia, where both groups of women have low unemployment rates.

```{r}
base_25_64 <-
  clean_data |>
  filter(country != "Luxembourg")

plot_NF_all_data <-
  base_25_64 |>
  filter(sex == "female", edu == "tertiary", age == "25-64") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = birth, values_from = unemp_rate) |>
  filter(!is.na(`native-born`), !is.na(`foreign-born`)) |>
  mutate(region_group = if_else(
    region %in% c("North America", "Oceania", "Western Europe", "Northern Europe"),
    "North America, Oceania, Western & Northern Europe",
    "Latin America, Southern & Eastern Europe"
  ))

ggplot(plot_NF_all_data, aes(x = `native-born`, y = `foreign-born`, colour = region_group)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Graph2: Unemployment rates of native-born and foreign-born\ntertiary-educated women aged 25-64",
    x = "Native-born (%)",
    y = "Foreign-born (%)",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "The diagonal line indicates equal unemployment rates for foreign-born and native-born women."
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = country), size = 2.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "North America, Oceania, Western & Northern Europe" = "blue",
    "Latin America, Southern & Eastern Europe" = "red"
  )) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### Graph3: Gap in unemployment rates between foreign-born and native-born tertiary-educated women aged 25–64

Graph 3 shows more clearly the gap between the unemployment rates of foreign-born and native-born women in each country, namely, the vertical distance between each point and the diagonal line in Graph 2. As shown in Graph 3, the rankings of the two regional groups are somewhat intermixed, but overall, the blue countries (major immigration destinations) tend to have smaller gaps. One point worth further consideration is that the three countries with the smallest gaps, Australia, the United States and New Zealand, are all non-European countries. Canada, another North American country, also has a gap smaller than that of most European countries. These results suggest that, beyond whether a country is a traditional immigration destination, we may also consider the differences between Europe and other regions, that is, whether conditions in Europe lead to a different pattern.

```{r}
gap_table <-
  plot_NF_all_data |>
  mutate(gap_pp = round(`foreign-born` - `native-born`, 1))

ggplot(gap_table, aes(x = gap_pp, y = reorder(country, gap_pp), fill = region_group)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = gap_pp), hjust = -0.2, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "North America, Oceania, Western & Northern Europe" = "blue",
    "Latin America, Southern & Eastern Europe" = "red"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(
    title = "Graph3: Gap in unemployment rates between foreign-born and native-born\ntertiary-educated women aged 25–64",
    x = "Foreign-born minus native-born (percentage points)",
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
